transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-12 15:00 UTC | Duration: 54m
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Diego (Redwood SE), Priya (NovaScale Head of ML), Evan (Platform), Rita (Security)

Summary (auto): technical deep dive on KV cache eviction and prefix reuse within long-context workloads. Discussed root causes (memory pressure, shard sizing, prefix collision), implications for batching/throughput, and mitigation strategies (pinning, reserve pools, eviction thresholds). Agreed on pilot benchmark and follow-ups.

Topics: KV cache eviction; paging & long context; prefix reuse and hash collisions; batching interaction with KV reuse; quantization effects on KV size; Dedicated vs Hosted tradeoffs; VPC/network and audit log concerns.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya: hey everyone thanks for joining, um this is Maya from Redwood, I'm the AE on the account, and with me is Diego who's our systems SE. you all wanna do quick intros?
[00:08] Priya: yeah sure, I'm Priya, Head of ML at NovaScale. Evan is our platform lead and Rita covers security for us. main pain: our prod chat assistants are seeing unexpected latency spikes and high token cost when users hit long conversations, we think KV eviction and re-computation is a big factor.
[00:22] Diego: hey, Diego here, I work on our serving runtime. quick note: we'll dig into eviction reasons and config knobs, and try to map to your traces.
[00:30] Evan: thanks, we also have a POC running on Dedicated infra and some traffic on hosted; want to understand whether to move everything to dedicated or tune hosted first.
[00:40] Rita: hi, short security intro - we need SOC2 + KMS integration and audit trails; any design we pick needs to keep keys customer-managed in VPC.
[00:50] Diego: understood. ok let's jump in. Priya can you give 2 minutes on workload shape?
[00:55] Priya: sure, so we have three main personas: quick QAs (short context), analyst flows (11k token notes, lots of prefix reuse across sessions), and support chat where users chain long contexts up to 90k tokens. prefix reuse is common because customers reference the same documents across threads; so we see repeated prefixes but with some variation.
[01:18] Diego: got it. so two things that usually cause eviction: net memory pressure (too many concurrent sessions / batch windows), and high cardinality of KV keys leading to inefficient caching. also prefix reuse can be counter-intuitive: if prefixes vary by minor tokens we treat them as different keys and can't reuse.
[01:36] Evan: that matches. we see spikes when we run batch exports; evictions line up with our nightly sync jobs that push bulk indexing.
[01:45] Diego: yep bulk jobs cause transient memory pressure and cause LRU evictions. our runtime uses segmented shards per GPU, each shard has a reserve and soft limit. if reserve is too small relative to your working set, we hit paging/eviction.
[02:00] Priya: what about paging? we get logs referencing paging and then huge CPU overhead.
[02:05] Diego: paging in our context is when we flush KV pages to local SSD (or host memory) — that adds I/O latency during retrieval. two immediate mitigations: increase in-memory shard size or reduce per-request KV footprint via prefix canonicalization and prompt engineering (reduce token variance).
[02:22] Rita: is there any data residency issue if cache spills to local disk? we need disk encryption and auditability.
[02:27] Maya: good flag. for Private / Dedicated we support encrypted local disks and KMS/HSM integration; we can provide audit logs for cache read/write events. we'll send the diagram.
[02:36] Priya: ok, can you walk through specific root causes you see in our traces?
[02:40] Diego: looking at the traces you shared — first, your prefix distribution is heavy-tailed: top 5% prefixes account for 60% of hits but there's a long tail of low-frequency prefixes that bloat the cache. second, concurrent batch windows are wide — batching improves throughput but holds more KV entries in memory until the batch completes, which increases peak memory. third, quantized key sizes: when models are quantized aggressively the KV element size shrinks, but we saw misaligned alignments in your quant path that doubled memory in some cases due to padding.
[03:10] Evan: wait misaligned quantization padding — can you expand?
[03:12] Diego: yeah, so some quant backends pack KV tensors in fixed block sizes; if your model's key dims aren't multiples of the block, we pad, and padding can increase per-entry size. combination with lots of small prefixes -> significant overhead.
[03:25] Priya: hmm that explains some numbers. is there a fix?
[03:28] Diego: options: 1) use a quant profile that aligns block sizes better for your model dims; 2) change model compilation kernels to use packed representations (we can do this for Dedicated); 3) logical coalescing of similar prefixes to reduce cardinality.
[03:42] Rita: for coalescing, is there any risk of leaking different user contexts into same cache key?
[03:47] Diego: good point — you must ensure canonicalization doesn't merge private prefixes across tenants. for multi-tenant customers we recommend tenant-scoped cache keys and a hashing scheme that includes tenant id plus canonicalized prefix fingerprint.
[03:58] Priya: what about prefix reuse: we have document IDs and often a small edit at the end — how do we get reuse?
[04:05] Diego: prefix canonicalization heuristics: strip trailing whitespace, normalize punctuation, optionally truncate to semantic boundary (end of sentence) and use a rolling fingerprint (e.g., SHA1 of normalized tokens). you can store mapping from docID+offset -> canonical prefix key so small edits don't create new keys. that's a design we typically prototype in the eval layer.
[04:25] Evan: sounds like extra complexity on our side. is there an automated approach?
[04:29] Diego: we can supply a lightweight library that does normalization and fingerprinting; Diego: (laugh) that's on me to drop in the repo.
[04:34] Maya: another lever is reserve pools and eviction thresholds — you can pin top-N prefixes in a hot pool that never get evicted unless operator-reset. that helps when you have a predictable hotset.
[04:44] Priya: we do know top docs — could pin them. what's the tradeoff for pinning?
[04:48] Diego: pins consume memory permanently so they reduce capacity for the rest of the working set; best for small hot sets (<5% of entries). Also need eviction policy for when pinned set changes.
[04:58] Priya: earlier you mentioned shard sizing — what should we set for our 3-GPU dedicated cluster?
[05:03] Diego: for your workload I'd recommend increasing per-shard soft limit by 30% from defaults and enable a 10% reserve headroom. also tune batch windows: reduce max batching latency to lower peak memory at cost of small throughput loss. we can provide a recommended config after we analyze full traces.
[05:20] Evan: any runtime flags we should flip immediately?
[05:22] Diego: yes: enable prefix-canonicalization hook (we can enable at the router), set eviction_policy to lfu+ttl for supporting long-tail reuse, and set reserve_pool to 10%.
[05:33] Priya: lfu? we thought LRU was default.
[05:35] Diego: default's LRU but LFU favors frequently reused prefixes — since you have a heavy head LFU is better. caution: LFU requires additional counters which are small overhead.
[05:45] Rita: about security — if we pin keys and keep them in-memory, are they visible to host admins?
[05:50] Maya: for Dedicated we support tenant-isolated VMs and we can encrypt page cache; keys are only stored in process memory and access is logged. Rita: ok we need documentation on audit events.
[06:00] Priya: can you explain eviction storms? we saw cascades where many sessions recompute long context after eviction causing CPU/latency spikes.
[06:09] Diego: eviction storms occur when multiple sessions access the same evicted prefix and re-populate simultaneously. mitigation: use asynchronous backfill with an exclusive lock or singleflight pattern so one request rebuilds and others wait or read a transient miss. also increase retry jitter on clients to avoid thundering herd.
[06:28] Evan: do you support cross-session KV sharing (like across user sessions if doc is public)?
[06:33] Diego: yes, that's supported but you must decide tenant scoping. For public docs you can share; for private docs, use tenant scoping. sharing increases reuse and reduces overall memory but raises privacy considerations.
[06:44] Priya: what about paging to SSD: our ops team prefers not to use local disk for any secret material.
[06:50] Diego: we can avoid paging by increasing memory headroom or using remote memory caches in your VPC (we have an optional memory-tier using Redis-style stores, but it's network-bound). For on-prem, we can provision nodes with larger RAM to avoid spill.
[07:05] Priya: can you quantify latency cost of a page hit?
[07:08] Diego: local SSD page hit ~5-15ms variability plus CPU to deserialize; remote memory (VPC) adds 2-10ms network depending on region; a full recompute of KV for long context can be hundreds of ms to multiple seconds depending on model.
[07:23] Evan: and what about batching — you said it holds entries longer; is there a way to get throughput without increasing eviction?
[07:30] Diego: yes smaller batch windows and adaptive batching: increase batch size during idle and shrink when memory pressure is high. also prefix-aware batching: group requests by prefix to maximize reuse within batch so you don't bring lots of new keys into memory.
[07:45] Priya: prefix-aware batching sounds great, how hard is that to implement?
[07:48] Diego: moderate; we can route requests by fingerprint before forming batches — Diego: (typing) we already have an experimental routing hook for that.
[07:55] Rita: on compliance again — logs for cache access, is that per-token or per-key? we don't want PII in logs.
[08:02] Maya: logs can be aggregated to key-level fingerprint only; we can redact content. will share the logging schema.
[08:08] Priya: any impact from model switch/rollouts? we plan A/B model rollouts and worry about cache misses after switch.
[08:15] Diego: model architecture changes that change KV shape or tokenization will invalidate cache. approach: warm the cache by replaying top trafficked prefixes in a canary rollout, or use model-compatibility mapping layer that maps old fingerprint to new when compatible.
[08:30] Evan: is there a way to measure hit-rate improvements from our changes?
[08:33] Diego: yes our console has per-prefix hit-rate metrics, per-shard memory pressure, and eviction traces. we'll give you a dashboard template to track Hits/Misses, EvictionRate, PageHits, and RecomputeLatency.
[08:46] Priya: what's the recommended pilot? Dedicated or Hosted?
[08:50] Diego: given your need for KMS and strict audit, Dedicated (or Private VPC) is a better fit for the pilot; Dedicated also lets us change kernel/quant paths and pack representations. Hosted can be tuned but has limits for kernel-level changes.
[09:02] Priya: cost tradeoffs? Dedicated is more expensive but might drop unit compute cost by 20-30% if we avoid recomputes?
[09:09] Maya: right, Dedicated is higher base cost but better predictable throughput and you save on re-compute token costs; we'll model it in the pilot.
[09:16] Evan: ok next steps?
[09:18] Maya: recap: Diego will analyse eviction logs and produce recommended runtime config + canonicalization lib. Priya will share more traces and top prefixes. Maya will send pilot pricing and SOC2/network docs. we schedule pilot kickoff next week.
[09:32] Priya: agreed. any immediate low-effort wins?
[09:35] Diego: enable prefix canonicalization hook, change eviction_policy to LFU+TTL, and pin top-50 prefixes — we can enable these quickly on Dedicated.
[09:45] Rita: and please redact any user text in logs before sharing.
[09:48] Maya: yes we'll follow best practices.
[09:50] Evan: thanks everyone, this was super helpful.
[09:53] Maya: great, we'll follow up with the artifacts and a proposed timeline.
